title: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
text: Adversaries email malicious attachments such as documents, archives or executables to gain a first foothold. Opening the file usually launches a macro, script or dropper that fetches further payloads.
mitigations: Detonate attachments in a sandbox before delivery
Block Office macros from internet-sourced files
Give users a one-click way to report suspicious mail

title: User Execution: Malicious File
text: The attacker relies on a person opening or running a file that looks legitimate, such as a fake invoice, installer or update. Execution then hands control to the embedded malicious code.

title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
text: Attackers abuse PowerShell to run commands, download payloads and execute code directly in memory. Encoded commands, hidden windows and download cradles are typical indicators.
mitigations: Turn on PowerShell script block logging

title: Data Encrypted for Impact
text: Ransomware encrypts files and drops ransom notes to disrupt availability and extort victims. Signs include mass file modification, renamed extensions and high-entropy file contents.
mitigations: Limit write access to shared drives
Deploy canary files to detect mass encryption early

title: Inhibit System Recovery
text: Adversaries delete shadow copies, backups and recovery settings so that victims cannot restore data after encryption or destruction.
mitigations: Protect backup systems with separate credentials
Alert on shadow copy deletion commands

title: Boot or Logon Autostart: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
text: Malware adds entries to registry run keys or the startup folder so that it launches again after each logon or reboot.
mitigations: Monitor autorun registry keys for changes

title: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
text: Adversaries create scheduled tasks or cron jobs to run malicious code repeatedly, for persistence or to execute at a chosen time.
mitigations: Limit task scheduling rights to administrators

title: Valid Accounts
text: Attackers use legitimate credentials obtained through phishing, leaks or guessing to blend in with normal activity and bypass many controls.
mitigations: Detect impossible travel and anomalous logins

title: Brute Force
text: Adversaries guess passwords by repeatedly trying credentials against services such as SSH, RDP or web logins. Telltale signs are many failed attempts from one source with regular timing.
mitigations: Apply account lockout and rate limiting

title: OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
text: Attackers read the memory of the LSASS process to harvest credentials that can be reused for lateral movement.
mitigations: Run LSASS as a protected process
Alert on unusual handle access to lsass.exe

title: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
text: Adversaries log in to other systems over RDP using valid credentials to move laterally inside a network.
mitigations: Restrict RDP to hardened jump hosts

title: Network Service Discovery
text: Adversaries scan hosts for open ports and reachable services to plan their next move. Sequential port probing with a SYN followed by a reset is a common scan pattern.
mitigations: Segment networks to limit reachable services
Use IDS rules for scan behaviour
Block scanning sources at the perimeter

title: Network Denial of Service
text: Attackers flood a target with traffic such as SYN or UDP floods to exhaust bandwidth or connection tables and make a service unavailable.
mitigations: Use upstream DDoS scrubbing or a CDN

title: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
text: Malware hides command-and-control traffic inside ordinary HTTP or HTTPS. Periodic beacons to rarely seen domains are a common indicator.
mitigations: Force egress through an inspecting proxy

title: Dynamic Resolution: Domain Generation Algorithms
text: Malware generates many pseudo-random domain names to find its controller, producing bursts of failed DNS lookups.
mitigations: Alert on NXDOMAIN spikes per host

title: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
text: Stolen data is sent out through the same channel used for command and control, often after being staged and compressed.
mitigations: Alert on large or unusual outbound transfers

title: Exfiltration Over Web Service
text: Adversaries upload data to legitimate web services such as cloud storage so the traffic blends in with normal usage.
mitigations: Apply CASB controls and egress baselines

title: Process Injection
text: Malicious code is run inside the address space of another process to evade detection and inherit its privileges.
mitigations: Enable attack surface reduction rules for injection APIs

title: Obfuscated Files or Information
text: Adversaries pack, encrypt or encode payloads to hide them from static analysis. Packed executables show high-entropy sections and few readable imports.
mitigations: Unpack in a sandbox for analysis
Use YARA rules for known packers
Block unsigned executables in temp directories

title: Ingress Tool Transfer
text: Attackers bring additional tools or payloads into a compromised environment, frequently with built-in utilities that fetch files from the internet.
mitigations: Monitor downloads written to temp directories

title: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
text: Adversaries turn off or reconfigure security software so that later stages run unobserved.

title: Exploit Public-Facing Application
text: Attackers exploit flaws in internet-facing applications to gain initial access, for example through injection or remote code execution.
mitigations: Place a WAF in front of web apps

title: Indicator Removal
text: Adversaries delete logs or alter timestamps to remove evidence of their activity.
mitigations: Forward logs off-host in real time

title: Drive-by Compromise
text: Visiting a compromised or malicious website silently exploits the browser or tricks the visitor into running a payload.

title: Injection
text: Untrusted input is sent to an interpreter as part of a command or query, letting attackers read or change data or run commands.

title: Broken Access Control
text: Users can act outside their intended permissions, for example by changing an identifier in a URL to reach another person's records.
mitigations: Log and alert on access-control failures

title: Identification and Authentication Failures
text: Weak login, session or recovery mechanisms let attackers impersonate users through guessing, stuffing or session theft.

title: Playbook: Ransomware response
text: Contain fast, preserve evidence, then eradicate and recover from clean backups. Do not pay before legal and leadership review.
steps: Isolate the affected host with EDR network containment (do not power it off)
Capture memory and a process list before any reboot
Disable the affected user account and rotate credentials
Scope spread using file-share and authentication logs
Restore from clean offline backups only after eradication

title: Playbook: Malicious attachment or phishing response
text: Find every recipient, remove the message, and treat any host that opened the file as compromised until proven otherwise.
steps: Quarantine the message from all mailboxes
Isolate hosts where the attachment was opened
Block sender, URLs and file hash at gateway and EDR
Reset credentials for users who opened the file
Collect the sample for sandbox analysis

title: Playbook: DDoS response
text: Protect availability first: absorb, filter, then trace the traffic pattern.
steps: Enable SYN cookies and connection rate limits on the affected tier
Engage the CDN or upstream scrubbing provider
Filter or blackhole the top offending source ranges
Scale out critical services and shed non-essential load
Keep packet captures for post-incident analysis

title: Playbook: Credential attack response
text: Stop the guessing, then check whether any attempt succeeded.
steps: Block the source address and enable rate limiting
Check authentication logs for a success after the failures
Force password reset and MFA on targeted accounts
Restrict the exposed service to VPN or a jump host
Review other services for the same source

title: Playbook: Reconnaissance and port scan response
text: Scans are rarely harmful alone but often precede an intrusion, so verify exposure and watch the source.
steps: Confirm which scanned ports are actually exposed
Block or rate-limit the scanning source
Search for follow-up exploitation attempts from the same source
Close unneeded services and tighten segmentation

title: Playbook: Suspicious executable triage
text: Treat unknown high-entropy binaries as hostile until analysed in isolation.
steps: Move the file to quarantine and record its hashes
Detonate in a sandbox to observe network and file behaviour
Search the estate for the same hash and file name
Block the hash and any extracted network indicators

title: Playbook: Data exfiltration response
text: Confirm whether data really left, identify what it was, and cut the channel.
steps: Identify the destination and block it at the proxy or firewall
Determine which data stores and accounts were accessed
Preserve proxy, DNS and NetFlow logs
Engage legal and privacy teams if personal data is involved
